background.definition: Constipation is defined as the passing of delayed or infrequent firm stools that occurs with pain and excessive straining. Functional constipation is constipation where there is no organic cause to the symptoms and it accounts for 95% of cases of constipation in children.

list.listitem: Reported in up to one-third of children aged 6 to 12 years during any given year.
Highly variable: studies report 0.7% to 29.6%, with a median 8.9%.
Highest prevalence of functional constipation is in preschool-age children (2-5 years old) with median age of onset is 2.3 years of age.
No difference is seen in the prevalence of constipation between boys and girls.
Constipation accounts for 3% of visits to the primary care physician and up to 25% of referrals to the pediatric gastroenterologist.
It costs the healthcare system three times more when managing children with constipation compared to children without constipation.
Constipation usually occurs between 2-5 years of age and is seen with transition to solid foods, during toilet training or with entry to school.
Functional constipation is most commonly caused by painful bowel movements, with resultant voluntary withholding of feces by a child to avoid further painful defecation.
Painful defecation causes a child to withhold stool. This in turn increases water absorption in the colon and makes the stool firmer.
The rectum dilates and loses muscular tone, causing the stool to increase in diameter. The stool becomes more difficult to pass and the urge to defecate decreases..
With time, the accumulation of stool causes a decrease in gastric emptying, results in abdominal distention, abdominal pain and nausea.
Encopresis occurs when loose stool leaks around the fecal impaction in the dilated rectum.

A thorough history and physical exam are sufficient to diagnose children with functional constipation in most cases. ,
C
Fever, abdominal distension, bloody diarrhea, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, or poor weight gain are symptoms that cause concern for constipation from an organic disorder. C
History of stool-withholding behavior reduces the likelihood of an organic disorder. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Passage of meconium >48 h after delivery; failure to thrive, fever, bloody diarrhea, bilious vomiting, empty rectum, tight sphincter, narrow stools. See chapter on Hirschsprung's disease

Differential.Differential_Name: Spinal cord abnormalities: tethered cord; myelomeningocele; spinal cord tumor
Differential.Differential_Features: Altered lower extremity reflexes; absent anal wink , absent cremasteric reflex, tight anal sphincter, hair patches/pits/dimples, scoliosis
Diarrhea, failure to thrive, rash, fever, pneumonia
Renal stones, bone pain, confusion, personality changes, bradycardia, hyperreflexia

Differential.Differential_Name: Antacids, anticholinergics, antidepressants, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder medications, chemotherapy, diuretics (dehydration), iron intake, heavy metal toxicity (i.e., lead poisoning), opiates, phenobarbital, sucralfate (Carafate), vitamin D toxicity
Imperforate anus or anal stenosis; anteriorly displaced anus
Differential.Differential_Features: Abnormal position of anus on physical exam

list.listitem:
Rome IV criteria for constipation: 2 or more of the following occurring at least once per week for at least 1 month and the symptoms cannot be explained by another medical condition:
Less than 2 defecations in the toilet per week in a child > 4 years of age At least 1 episode of fecal incontinence per week after acquisition of toileting skills History of retentive posturing or excessive volitional stool retention History of painful or hard bowel movements Presence of a large fecal mass in the rectum History of large-diameter stools that may obstruct the toilet
Functional constipation is a clinical diagnosis based on the ROME IV criteria and no additional testing is required in patients without red flag signs or symptoms.
Confirm child passed meconium within 48 hours after birth and the pattern of bowel movements as an infant.

Be alert for "red flags" suggesting an organic disorder. Red flags include failure to pass meconium in the first 48 hours of life, constipation since birth/first few weeks of life, "ribbon stools," abdominal distension with vomiting, and inadequate weight gain.

Red flag symptoms also include abnormal growth parameters, fever, abnormal appearance/position/patency of anus, presence of fistula, fissures, absent anal wink, abdominal distension, asymmetric gluteal folds, discolored skin/nevi/sinus/hairy patch/lipoma/central pit in lumbosacral area, scoliosis, deformity of lower limbs, abnormal lower limb reflexes, abnormal neuromuscular examination, bilious vomiting.
Medications and dietary history must be assessed as a potential cause of constipation.
It is important to address social history, family history, prior therapies, medications and behavior as it may guide treatment outcomes.

Management of chronic functional constipation is multifactorial and involves a complex interplay of physical, and psychosocial factors, including the personal characteristics of the child and the environment in which they live.

There is insufficient evidence to support a digital rectal exam for the diagnosis of constipation in a child with no red flag signs or symptoms. However a digital rectal exam may be performed if organic causes are suspected.
Additional diagnostic testing is not usually required in children with constipation who do not present with red flag signs or symptoms. , ,
Psychological factors can result in functional constipation in patients with autism and attention deficit disorders.
Generally, diagnostic testing such as abdominal X-ray are not necessary in children with functional constipation. ,,, C
Rectal biopsy and anomanometry should be done if Hirshprung's disease is suspected. Anorectal manometry alone does not exclude Hirschsprung's disease.

The 2014 ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN guidelines do not recommend colon transit studies to diagnose functional constipation; they may be helpful to distinguish functional constipation from functional non-retentive fecal incontinence.
If rectal exam is too traumatic or is refused, or shows no fecal impaction, abdominal X-ray may be considered.
Consider testing for celiac disease and hypothyroidism if intractable constipation not responding to treatment.
See algorithm in and 2.
Polyethylene glycol 3350 is effective for treatment of childhood fecal impaction (1.0 to 1.5 g/kg/day) and maintenance (0.4 g/kg/day) in children with constipation.,,, A
Children <6 months old have generally good response to dietary intervention with sorbitol containing juices such as prune juice (1-3 mL/kg/day). B
Additional fluid or fiber intake beyond what is recommended has not been consistently shown to resolve constipation. A

There is insufficient evidence to support increased physical activity or probiotic use alleviates constipation.
A

Some children with functional constipation may benefit with behavioral health intervention from a child psychologist. B Behavioral interventions are effective for long-term treatment of encopresis with constipation. A
Consider a trial of eliminating cow's milk from the diet of children with constipation unresponsive to medical and behavioral management. B
First step in managing pediatric constipation is determining and treating disimpaction. Disimpaction can be done with oral or rectal medications, including enemas. See .

PEG 3550 is the first-line recommendation for disimpaction. PEG 3550 is dosed at 1-1.5 g/kg/day for disimpaction with 6-8 oz fluids for 2-6 days. Enemas can be used as second-line if PEG 3550 not available for 3-6 days.
If treatment at home with oral and rectal medications is unsuccessful, children may need to be hospitalized where PEG 3550 can be given via a nasogastric tube, or manual disimpaction can be done.

Following disimpaction (or if disimpaction is not indicated), first-line maintenance therapy for constipation is also PEG 3550 with starting dose at 0.4 g/kg/day. PEG 3550 can be titrated to achieve goal of soft daily bowel movements. If PEG 3550 not available, alternative first line agent for maintenance therapy is lactulose (1-3 mL/kd/day). See .
Treatment should continue for at least 2 months and be gradually discontinued once constipation has resolved.
For children <6 months, consider disimpaction with glycercin suppositories instead of enema. For maintenance therapy, begin with sorbitol containing juices such as prune (1-3 mL/kg/day).

The 2014 ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN guidelines recommend that milk of magnesia, mineral oil, and stimulant laxatives are second-line treatments and may be considered. Routine use of lubiprostone, linaclotide, and prucalopride are not recommended in the absence of randomized trials in children.
Additional fluid or fiber intake beyond what is recommended has not been consistently shown to resolve constipation.
There is insufficient evidence to support increased physical activity or probiotic use alleviates constipation.
Behavioral interventions plus laxative therapy, rather than laxative therapy alone, improves continence in children with encopresis with constipation.
Some children with functional constipation may benefit with behavioral health intervention from child psychologist.
The 2014 ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN guidelines recommend demystification, explanation, and guidance for toilet training for children at least 4 years of age.
Biofeedback therapy is not recommended by 2014 ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN guidelines.
The 2014 ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN guidelines recommend normal fiber intake, normal fluid intake, and normal physical activity for children with functional constipation.
Cow's milk may cause constipation in some children: consider a trial of withholding cow's milk in children unresponsive to other medical and behavioral management.
Sorbitol in prune, pear, and apple juices increases water content of stools.
Recommended daily fluid intake for children varies by age. For ages 1-3 years old, 4 cups of fluid per day; for ages 4-8 years old, 5 cups per day; and for older children, 7-8 cups per day.
No added benefit of physiotherapy to usual care (education, diet advice, toilet training, medications).
Maintenance therapy should be continued for a minimum of at least two months or additional 1 month after response to treatment.
Consultation with a pediatric gastroenterologist is necessary when therapy fails, when concern regarding organic disease exists, or when management is complex.
Treatment failure is considered as not achieving regular bowel movements after 3 months of adequate therapy.
Referral to a mental health provider for behavior modification or counseling for the family may be helpful, especially when treatment failure is encountered.
See for disimpaction medications.
PEG 3550 can be given via nasogastric tube in the hospital setting at starting dose of 10 mL/kg/hr and can be titrated up to 40 mL/kg/hr in 10-20 mL increments.
Up to half of children with functional constipation continue to require therapy after 5 years of treatment. B
One-quarter of children with chronic constipation remain constipated into adolescence and adulthood despite intensive therapeutic management . B
Consistent follow up is recommended to ensure adequate response to therapy. C
Educate parents that fecal soiling from encopresis is not a defiant or willful action by the child.
An unhurried time on the toilet after meals is recommended to utilize the gastrocolic reflex.
Positive reinforcement with a diary and point system for successful bowel movements can be used for behavioral modification.

feature.caption: Medications for Clean-Out/Disimpaction.
feature.feature_body:
Medication Side Effects/Comments
Infants <1 Year Old
Glycerin suppositories No side effects
Enema: 6 mL/kg up to 4.5 oz (135 cc) If enemas are considered, administer first in doctor's office
Children >1 Year Old
Rapid Clean-Out
Polyethylene glycol 3350 powder (Miralax): 1-1.5 g/kg/day (Mix 17g/ 8oz of water or juice) once or divided doses bid x3 days Superior palatability and acceptance by children
Enema: 6 mL/kg up to 4.5 oz (135 cc) every 12-24 h ×1-3 Invasive; risk of mechanical trauma
Magnesium citrate: <6y: 1-3 mL/kg/d; 6-12 y: 100-150 mL/d; >12 y: 150-300 mL/d in single or divided doses Hypermagnesemia
Hypertonic phosphate enemas (for children older than 2 years) Abdominal cramping; risk of hyperphosphatemia
Combination: enema, suppository, oral laxative See "enemas" above
Day 1: Enema q 12-24 h Abdominal cramping, diarrhea, hypokalemia
Day 2: Bisacodyl suppository (10 mg) q 12-24 h Abdominal cramping, diarrhea, hypokalemia
Day 3: Bisacodyl tablet (5 mg) q 12-24 h
Repeat 3 day cycle if needed ×1-2
Oral/NG: Polyethylene glycol electrolyte solution (Golytely or Nulytely) 25 mL/kg/h up to 1000 mL/h ×4 h/day) Nausea, cramping, vomiting, bloating, aspiration; large volume; usually requires nasogastric tube and hospitalization to administer
Slower Clean-Out
Polyethylene glycol 3350 powder (Miralax): 1 g/kg/day (Mix 17g/ 8oz of water or juice) once or divided doses bid Superior palatability and acceptance by children
Mineral oil: 1-3 mL/kg/d (up to 1 oz a day/year of age, up to 240 mL daily) Lipid pneumonia if aspirated
Senna: 2-6 y: 2.5-7.5 mL/d; 6-12 y: 5-15 mL/d. Consider IF polyethylene glycol not leading to disimpaction after 2 weeks Abdominal cramping; may not see output until dose 2 or 3
Magnesium citrate: <6 y: 1-3 mL/kg/d; 6-12 y: 100-150 mL/d; >12 y: 150-300 mL/d in single or divided doses Hypermagnesemia
